title: web: next features
description:
## Central vs local: which UI gets which feature

Per `docs/client-server-design.md` → Web UI topology, the SPA is deployed in two places with different capabilities:

- **Central read-only dashboard** (mvp-si5u): visualizations, drill-downs, shareable URLs, audit log views, external links. Read-only.
- **Local write-capable UI** (this epic): everything the central dashboard has, PLUS write actions (set/unset override, set vault, run puppet, view vault content).

When planning a feature here, decide up front whether it's read-only (belongs in BOTH surfaces, via shared SPA code) or write-capable (local UI only, gated on `capabilities.writes`). Write-action features (multi-host overrides, confirmation dialogs, vault-content viewer) are LOCAL-UI-ONLY and must not be mountable on the central deployment.

---

## Motivation

Some users prefer a browser-based interface over a CLI/TUI. Multi-host operations (selecting hosts, setting overrides, reviewing changes before applying) map naturally to browser interactions — checkboxes, dropdowns, confirmation dialogs — in a way that's harder to achieve in a terminal. The web UI effort exists to make fleetroll accessible to users who find the CLI friction too high.

## Web UI vs TUI: Feature Fit Analysis

**Web UI wins clearly:**
- Rich data visualization — sparklines, color-coded health bars, charts over time (puppet run history, TC job success rates)
- Clickable drill-downs — click a hostname → full detail page with audit log, override history, vault state, TC worker details
- Multi-host actions with confirmation dialogs — selecting a set of hosts, previewing a change, confirming (LOCAL UI ONLY — requires writes)
- Links to external systems — TC task URLs, GitHub override branch links, Bugzilla tickets in notes. Clickable in a browser, not a terminal
- Shareable views — send a URL with a filter/sort pre-applied (CENTRAL UI — only central has a shareable URL)
- Notes editing — inline editable text fields beat vim-in-a-popup for non-power users
- Multiple simultaneous views — multiple tabs with different filters

**TUI wins clearly:**
- SSH session speed — already in a terminal, no browser needed
- Low-latency keyboard navigation — faster for power users who know the bindings
- No build step, no Node, no browser — works anywhere Python runs
- Real-time updates — curses getch loop already polls at 200ms; web requires SSE/WebSockets
- Muscle memory — operators already running fleetroll commands all day

**Recommendation: build web UI features the TUI can't do well**
- Drill-down detail pages (audit log, override history, vault state, TC worker details per host)
- Audit log visualization
- External links (TC tasks, GitHub branches)
- Shareable filtered views (central dashboard only)

Don't try to replicate the live-updating host grid immediately (requires SSE/WebSockets, deferred). The read-only snapshot grid (mvp-kaw5.2) is right, but frame it as a 'dashboard you share' not a 'monitor you stare at'.

The TUI remains the operator's tool; the web UI lowers the barrier for users who find the CLI friction too high.

title: Expose override-aware worker identity and TC evidence in monitor JSON
description:
Expose override-aware worker pool identity and Taskcluster evidence in host monitor JSON, while preserving the Puppet role field.

Motivation

Moonshot Medic selected ms017 for reset while it had a WORKER_TYPE_OVERRIDE targeting gecko-t-linux-talos-2404-tc-v115. The Puppet role remained gecko_t_linux_2404_talos. We have not established which stale or mismatched observation caused the selection; consumers need enough structured evidence to distinguish role, intended pool, observed configuration, and Taskcluster activity instead of inferring a pool from the role.

Current code

- fleetroll/commands/monitor/entry.py emits only the latest host audit for --once --json and the initial JSON snapshot; it loads TC observations and override metadata but does not include them in the JSON payload.
- monitor/data.py already computes a pool filter field from TC data, but this is separate from role and is not included by the raw JSON path.
- gather_tc.py already resolves WORKER_TYPE_OVERRIDE and collected worker identities. Reuse these semantics rather than inventing another role/pool resolver.

Scope

Add an additive, documented JSON contract with explicit fields for:

1. Configured worker type: role default with an active WORKER_TYPE_OVERRIDE applied, including resolution source and unknown/unresolved status.
2. Observed worker identity read from host configuration: provisioner, worker type, worker group, worker ID, collection status, and observation timestamp. This does not claim the worker process is running.
3. Taskcluster evidence: identity/pool queried, observation timestamp, last activity, and lookup/result status. Keep stale or mismatched evidence visible rather than presenting it as current inactivity in the intended pool.

Keep the existing role value as the Puppet role. Final field names and nesting can follow project conventions; suggested names discussed were configured_worker_type, observed_worker_identity, and taskcluster. Prefer JSON scope first; a visible pool column can be considered separately.

Acceptance criteria

- Existing host audit fields and role meaning remain compatible; new fields are additive.
- JSON exposes configured, host-observed, and TC-observed identities with timestamps/statuses sufficient for Medic to match activity to the correct pool.
- An applied override such as ms017's identifies gecko-t-linux-talos-2404-tc-v115 rather than deriving the pool solely from gecko_t_linux_2404_talos.
- Override deployed but not applied, failed host audits, missing/failed identity collection, missing TC records, stale TC observations, and pool mismatches are explicit and distinguishable from healthy/current observations.
- --once --json, initial follow-mode JSON, and subsequent JSON updates have consistent documented semantics; do not silently fall back to an old pool.
- Tests cover override/no-override hosts, successful and failed application/collection, missing or stale TC data, and mismatched identities. Document JSON examples and the migration path for automation consumers.

Consumer follow-up

Medic should validate matching pool identity and fresh activity evidence before automatic resets. This task supplies that evidence; changing Medic's reset decision or implementing a new display column is outside its initial scope. Related design context: mvp-d0kx (health/freshness/automation safety signals).

Requested outcome is a task only; no implementation has been authorized yet.

title: Add structured logging with structlog
description:
Current debug logging uses unstructured string formatting. Structured logging would improve production debugging and observability.

## Current State
```python
logger.debug(f'Auditing host {host}, timeout={timeout}')
```

## Proposed Pattern
```python
import structlog
logger = structlog.get_logger()

logger.info('audit_started', host=host, timeout=timeout)
logger.info('audit_complete', host=host, duration_ms=elapsed, success=True)
logger.warning('ssh_retry', host=host, attempt=2, error=str(e))
```

## Benefits
- Machine-parseable logs (JSON output option)
- Consistent field names across log entries
- Easy integration with log aggregation (ELK, Datadog, etc.)
- Context binding (add request_id, actor to all logs in a session)

## Implementation
1. Add structlog to dependencies
2. Configure processors (JSON for prod, console for dev)
3. Replace logger.debug/info calls with structured equivalents
4. Add context binding for actor, session_id

## Priority
P4 - Nice to have for production deployment, not blocking MVP functionality. Current logging is adequate for development.

title: Persist TC lookup attempts separately from successful worker observations
description:
Follow-up to mvp-khj3: persist per-host Taskcluster lookup attempts independently of the last successful worker observation.

Problem
Monitor JSON currently exposes the stored successful TC observation, but latest_lookup_status is unknown because gather tc does not retain failed attempts. A fresh retained success can conceal a later failed lookup or an attempted query against a different pool.

Scope
- Persist the latest per-host lookup attempt separately from successful TC worker observations, with bounded retention. Do not overwrite or refresh the last successful observation on failure.
- Record attempt timestamp, full queried identity (provisioner, worker type, group, ID) when resolved, resolution source, result status, and a concise sanitized error. Identity-unresolved attempts must be explicit and must not infer an old pool.
- Distinguish success, worker_missing, identity_unresolved, pool_query_failed, and task_lookup_failed. Represent ambiguous worker matches explicitly as well. Fan out pool-query failures to each affected requested host; preserve successful results for other hosts in partial batches.
- Expose latest_lookup alongside the last successful observation in monitor JSON. Preserve existing successful-record fields and timestamps, update/version the documented contract as needed, and emit follow updates on attempt-only changes.
- Existing databases migrate safely. Historical attempts remain unknown until another gather; never synthesize a successful attempt from a retained worker observation.
- Keep gather exit-status behavior and existing display consumers compatible. Changing Medic reset policy and adding TUI columns are outside scope.

Acceptance criteria
- A success followed by any failed lookup advances only attempt evidence; successful observation timestamp, activity, and identity remain unchanged.
- A pool/identity change followed by failure exposes the new attempted identity and the old successful identity distinctly; no fallback or inactivity claim for the intended pool.
- Missing/ambiguous workers, unresolved identity, pool API errors, task-status errors, partial batch success, and failure without any previous success are covered by meaningful storage and gather tests.
- Once JSON, initial follow snapshot, and subsequent updates expose consistent attempt/result semantics, including attempt-only updates and migration from legacy data.
- Documentation includes success-then-failure and pool-change-then-failure examples and explains lookup freshness versus successful-observation freshness and activity time.
close_reason: Persisted one latest completed TC lookup attempt per host independently of successful worker observations. Gather records queried identity, resolution source, timestamps, sanitized errors, and distinct success/unresolved/pool failure/missing/ambiguous/task failure outcomes, preserving prior successful evidence on failure and partial batches. Failed audits now block stale legacy-pool fallback. Monitor JSON schema v2 exposes independent lookup freshness and attempt-only follow updates; legacy migrations retain unknown attempts. Added storage, gather, migration, and JSON regression coverage; all 1494 tests and prek passed.

title: Investigate extended terminal colors (256 vs 16)
description:
Investigate using extended terminal color support for better visual distinction in the monitor display.

## Current State

Currently using 16 basic colors (COLOR_CYAN, COLOR_YELLOW, etc.) with doubled palette via A_REVERSE attribute. This limits visual design options.

## Investigation Areas

1. **256-color support**
   - Most modern terminals support 256 colors
   - Provides better gradations and more distinct colors
   - Can use color palette indices 0-255

2. **Detection**
   - Check TERM environment variable (xterm-256color, screen-256color, etc.)
   - Query curses.COLORS to see available color count
   - Graceful fallback to 16-color mode for older terminals

3. **Use cases**
   - More distinct role colors (currently cycling through limited palette)
   - Better status indication gradients (fresh → stale)
   - Improved help popup styling

## Implementation Considerations

- Use curses.COLORS to detect capability
- Define color schemes for both 16-color and 256-color modes
- Test on common terminal emulators (iTerm2, Terminal.app, tmux, screen)

## References

- curses.init_pair() supports color indices 0-255 when COLORS >= 256
- Standard 256-color palette: 0-15 (basic), 16-231 (216-color cube), 232-255 (grayscale)
close_reason: Implemented 256-color support with 8 distinct extended colors (orange, purple, pink, teal, maroon, gold, forest-green, orange-red). Combined with standard 7 colors gives 15 total (30 with reverse) - more than enough for 22 SHA values. Tested and working.

title: release-notes: assign beads by git commit (closed status in diff) instead of closed_at date
description:
Currently, release-notes assigns beads to versions by comparing `closed_at` date against the date range of each version's git commits. This can cause misattribution when a bead is closed on a date that falls in version X's window but its implementing commit lands in version Y's SHA range.

Alternative approach: use `git log --diff-filter=M -- .beads/issues.jsonl` to find the commit where each bead's status changed to 'closed', then assign the bead to whatever version range contains that commit SHA. This would keep bead assignment and commit assignment in the same coordinate system (git DAG) rather than mixing date-based and SHA-based attribution.

Design questions:
- Parse the diff output to detect status field changing to 'closed'
- Handle edge cases: bead closed in same commit as version bump, bead never committed, manual edits
- Consider performance: one git log per bead vs one pass over all .beads/issues.jsonl changes
close_reason: Implemented git-commit-based bead attribution via parse_bead_close_commits_from_diff and assign_beads_to_versions. Beads are now assigned to versions by scanning git log -p on .beads/issues.jsonl for status transitions to closed, using the same SHA ranges as commits. Falls back to date-based filtering for edge cases. Also fixed stats block labels (beads-covered, housekeeping row), bead type breakdown rendering, and sub-task suffix stripping in extract_bead_id.

title: Client/server: centralize scanning behind read-only API
description:
Centralize scanning (host-audit, tc-fetch, gh-fetch) behind a shared read-only HTTP API + SSE so N operators stop making N× scans. Keep writes on operator machines via direct SSH (operator's privileged key). Split the web UI into a central read-only dashboard and a local write-capable operator UI.

See `docs/client-server-design.md` for the full design — architecture, web UI topology, phase breakdown, and key decisions.

Invariants:
- Server pods carry a read-only SSH key; write routes are never mounted on the central deployment.
- Vault content never leaves the operator's machine; the server stores only SHA256.
- Local write-capable UI binds to 127.0.0.1 only; refuses to start otherwise when writes are enabled.

Phase beads under this epic cover: DataProvider abstraction, read-only central server, split web UI, shared notes, and K8s deploy + auth.

title: Phase 1: DataProvider abstraction (LocalProvider over db.py)
description:
Pure refactor, no server yet. Introduce a `DataProvider` protocol that abstracts the reads the TUI currently performs directly against `db.py`.

Scope:
- Create `fleetroll/data_provider.py` with the `DataProvider` protocol
- Implement `LocalProvider` wrapping existing `db.py` functions (`load_latest_records`, `load_tc_worker_data_from_db`, etc.)
- Refactor `MonitorDisplay` and `fleetroll/commands/monitor/entry.py` to consume a `DataProvider` instead of the db connection directly
- All existing behavior and tests unchanged

See `docs/client-server-design.md` → Phase 1.

AuditLogTailer now obtained via provider.make_tailer(). The commit() read-consistency hack moved into LocalProvider where it belongs. All 818 tests pass, prek clean. Swapping in RemoteProvider (Phase 2) is now a one-line constructor change in entry.py.

title: Phase 2: Read-only central server (FastAPI + Postgres + SSE + RemoteProvider)

Build the central server: FastAPI + uvicorn + sse-starlette, PostgreSQL for state, background scanning tasks with leader election via Postgres advisory lock. RemoteProvider on the client.

Scope:
- New package `fleetroll/server/`: `app.py`, `scanner.py`, `events.py`, `config.py`
- Read-only API endpoints (see `docs/client-server-design.md` → Key API Endpoints) — snapshot, observations SSE stream, tc-workers, github-refs, windows-pools, notes (read), sha-info, overrides, status, capabilities
- Write routes must NOT be mounted on this deployment (`enable_writes=false`)
- Server SSH key is read-only
- `RemoteProvider` using httpx (REST + SSE)
- `--server` flag on `host-monitor` selects RemoteProvider over LocalProvider
- New CLI: `fleetroll server --config server.toml`

Depends on Phase 1 (DataProvider).

title: Phase 2.5: Split web UI — local write-capable vs central read-only

Promote the existing fleetroll/commands/web/ app into the operator's write-capable UI. Central deployment stays read-only; the local UI gets write buttons using the operator's SSH key.

Scope:
- Add enable_writes: bool to the web app factory.
- Conditionally mount write routes: POST/DELETE override, POST vault, POST puppet-run, GET vault-content, wrapping the existing command functions.
- Integrate the loopback startup enforcement delivered by mvp-kaw5.4 before enabling local write routes. Implementation, documentation, and tests of that binding policy belong to mvp-kaw5.4.
- Add GET /api/v1/capabilities for SPA feature detection.
- Add SPA write-action components gated on capabilities.writes.

See docs/design/client-server-design.md, Web UI topology and Phase 2.5.

Depends on mvp-si5u.2 (central server) and mvp-kaw5.4 (loopback enforcement). The read-only host grid in mvp-kaw5.2 is already built. Central-server bearer-token authentication remains owned by mvp-si5u.5.

title: Phase 3: Shared notes + SHA info on server
description:
Move notes and SHA info from per-operator local DB to server-managed shared state.

Scope:
- Notes CRUD endpoints on server (POST/DELETE /api/v1/notes)
- Clients read/write notes via API when using RemoteProvider
- SHA info cache served from server (override content by SHA)
- Vault SHA info stays metadata-only on server (no content)

Ship the central server to K8s and harden it.

- Local mode kept as fallback

Depends on Phase 2. See `docs/client-server-design.md` → Phase 4.

title: Client-submitted audit observations after operator writes
description:
After an operator runs host-set-override, host-unset-override, host-set-vault, or host-run-puppet from their machine (CLI or local web UI), the effect should be visible in the shared central view without waiting for the next scheduled scan.

Proposal: the local write path runs an immediate local audit and POSTs the observation to the server via a new authenticated endpoint (for example POST /api/v1/observations). The server validates, persists, and fans out on SSE just like observations from its own scanner.

Security invariants unchanged: the server never writes to managed hosts; its SSH key stays read-only. Clients authenticate with their bearer token; submitted observations carry the operator identity for the audit trail. This bead applies the central authentication mechanism to the submission endpoint and tests rejection of missing or invalid credentials.

Design questions to resolve: schema for submitted observations, deduplication/ordering with server-scanner observations, trust model for operator-submitted data, operator attribution, and rate limiting.

Prerequisites:
- mvp-si5u.2 provides the central server and observation/SSE infrastructure.
- mvp-si5u.5 owns central bearer-token authentication. Authenticated submission must wait for that mechanism; server creation alone does not supply it. Reuse that mechanism rather than introducing a separate authentication policy.

title: host-unset-override: allow selective removal by commit
description:
Add source-commit selection to the population override-removal foundation in mvp-3vc.1, allowing operators to clean up overrides associated with completed test work.

Correct host model:
- Each supported host has one active override at its platform-specific path, not multiple active override files.
- Different hosts can have different override contents associated with one source commit.
- If host A originally received an override associated with commit A and later received a replacement associated with commit B, removing commit A must leave B's active override intact.

Scope and provenance decisions:
- Define exactly what source commit means before implementation: the repository commit containing the override artifact is distinct from the Puppet revision targeted or applied by that override, and from the override content SHA256. Document repository identity with the commit.
- Inventory existing override metadata and audit provenance first. Define an explicit, durable association from deployed override content to its source commit; decide whether additional metadata is necessary rather than prescribing a new file header up front.
- Resolve and validate commit input against the correct source repository. Define handling for abbreviated or ambiguous SHAs and unavailable repositories.
- Missing, malformed, ambiguous, or conflicting provenance must remain unknown and must not authorize removal. Define compatibility behavior for older overrides without provenance.
- Add commit selection through the existing override unset command, with final option names chosen during implementation. Preserve explicit host/file targeting and define composition with filters; combine supplied selectors by intersection rather than broadening the population.

Shared execution:
- Depend on and reuse mvp-3vc.1 for population selection, exact previews, observation timestamps/freshness, explicit confirmation, execution-time expected-content verification, removal, audit records, automatic refresh, exit statuses, and human/JSON results.
- Preview the matched source repository/commit, exact hostnames, and expected active override identities, plus unknown or excluded hosts.
- Never remove a newer replacement override based solely on historical deployment provenance. Already-absent content is an idempotent no-op.
- Document post-merge cleanup and recovery/redeployment using retained override content, keeping removal distinct from Puppet convergence.

Validation:
- Test several hosts with different override contents associated with the same source commit.
- Test A replaced by B on one host: selecting A must preserve B.
- Cover matching/nonmatching provenance, legacy or malformed records, ambiguous commits, empty matches, combined selectors, preview/confirmation, changes after preview, partial failures, audits, and refreshes.

Keep this bead open at P2. It adds a selector, not a second population-removal implementation or a multiple-overrides-per-host model.

title: Sync moonshot notes from master inventory Google Sheet
description:
Sync notes from the Moonshot master inventory Google Sheet into fleetroll's local data store so host records include the latest moonshot annotations.

## Background
The Moonshot master inventory Google Sheet contains notes and annotations about hosts that are maintained by the ops team. Currently these notes are not available in fleetroll, requiring engineers to cross-reference the sheet manually.

## Technical Approach
- Authenticate with the Google Sheets API (service account or OAuth)
- Read the relevant columns from the moonshot master inventory sheet
- Map sheet rows to hosts by hostname or other identifier
- Store synced notes in the fleetroll DB alongside host records
- Expose the notes in existing host views (monitor, audit output, etc.)

## Success Criteria
- Running a sync command pulls current notes from the sheet
- Notes appear on the correct host records in fleetroll
- Re-running sync updates changed notes without duplicating entries
- Hosts with no sheet entry are unaffected

## Considerations
- Sheet URL / ID and credentials need to be configurable
- Rate limits on Sheets API
- Graceful handling when sheet is unreachable
notes: Related: mvp-3oz imports the same Moonshot inventory notes from a local/exported document. Decide the authoritative source before implementation: use this bead for ongoing Google Sheets synchronization, or prefer mvp-3oz for a one-time/export-file workflow. Avoid maintaining two independent note sources without clear precedence.

title: Replace Args bag with typed dataclasses
description:
The Args class (cli.py:44-49) is a dynamic attribute bag that discards type information:

```python
class Args:
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        for key, value in kwargs.items():
            setattr(self, key, value)
```

Impact: No IDE completion, runtime AttributeError possible, unclear contracts between CLI and command functions.

Solution: Create typed definitions for each command's arguments.

**Option 1: TypedDict** (recommended)
Lightweight, good type checking, standard library. Args objects are created once and passed to commands, so mutability isn't a concern in practice.

**Option 2: Dataclasses with frozen=True**
If enforcing immutability is desired, though adds boilerplate overhead.

Commands needing typed args:
- HostAuditArgs
- HostMonitorArgs  
- OverrideShowArgs
- VaultShowArgs
- HostSetOverrideArgs
- HostSetVaultArgs
- HostUnsetOverrideArgs
- TcFetchArgs

title: host-monitor: make DATA field sortable by TC_DATA and HOST_DATA
description:
## Background
The DATA field in host-monitor shows combined task collector and host data age, but currently isn't sortable. Users cannot independently order by when task collector data was last updated (TC_DATA) versus when host data was last updated (HOST_DATA).

## Technical Approach
Add two new sort keys (TC_DATA and HOST_DATA) alongside existing sort modes (HOST, STATUS, ROLE, OBSERVATION_AGE). Each key should be associated with a sort function that extracts and compares the appropriate timestamp. Update the sort mode indicator to display these new options when available.

## Success Criteria
- User can cycle through sort modes including TC_DATA and HOST_DATA in interactive mode
- Rows are sorted correctly by task collector data age when TC_DATA is selected
- Rows are sorted correctly by host data age when HOST_DATA is selected
- Sort mode indicator displays the correct abbreviation (TC_DATA or HOST_DATA) when active
- Existing sort modes (HOST, STATUS, ROLE, OBSERVATION_AGE) continue to work

## Test Plan
- Add unit tests for sort key extraction for both TC_DATA and HOST_DATA
- Add integration tests verifying correct row ordering for TC_DATA and HOST_DATA sort modes
- Add TUI test verifying sort mode indicator displays TC_DATA and HOST_DATA when selected
- Verify no regression in existing sort modes

## Considerations
- Ensure DATA field parsing correctly extracts task collector vs host data timestamps
- Consider default sort order (ascending or descending) for age values
- Verify performance impact of additional sort key comparisons

title: host-run-puppet errors can exit silently without status or audit record
description:
Parent epic for making host-run-puppet predictable during rollouts. The August 20260805-worker_timing incident initially appeared silent because default batch execution emits no start/progress feedback and only prints captured remote output after each host completes. Separately, target run-puppet.sh wrappers intentionally retry until success, which is unsafe for an operator-triggered Fleetroll action.

Goal: Fleetroll runs one bounded attempt by default when the remote wrapper supports it, shows live batch status, and always records/report failures. Normal boot and worker wrapper behavior must retain retry-until-success semantics.

Child work:
- Add FLEETROLL_SINGLE_RUN support to Linux/macOS Puppet wrappers.
- Invoke and verify single-attempt mode in Fleetroll, failing fast if unsupported.
- Make batch progress visible independent of --quiet (except JSON).
- Ensure SSH exceptions/timeouts yield per-host audit records and nonzero results.

Source incident: 20260805-worker_timing rollout; hosts t-linux64-ms-016 and t-linux64-ms-046.
